turns.user: what's the GRE score validity period? thinking about taking it in november and then applying next fall
turns.assistant:
GRE scores are valid for five years from the test date. So a November test would still count for applications next fall, and for several cycles after that if you needed it.

The score report itself doesn't expire, but most graduate programs prefer scores from the last five years, and some will only consider more recent ones, so check each program's policy if you're applying later than planned.

turns.user: is there a cap on how many times i can take it

turns.user: and do schools only see the best score or all of them

Many programs say they'll consider your highest scores, while others look at the whole history. Some programs take the best of each section. Check the school's admissions page, because it often says how they handle multiple attempts.

turns.assistant:

Leetcode is good for keeping your coding fluent, so it's useful as a light daily habit rather than your main activity. System design books matter more if you're going for senior roles or your interviews include a design round. For mid-level backend, you'd probably spend the most time on the coding and a smaller amount on design.

A reasonable split is mocks two or three times a week, a short daily coding session, and one design topic each week.

turns.assistant:
Interviewing.io feels more real because the interviewers are working engineers, often at larger companies, and the feedback is more detailed. It costs money, though, and you pay per session.

Pramp pairs you with another candidate, so the interviewer is a peer rather than a professional. That's still useful for practice and it's free, but the feedback is usually less consistent.

If budget allows, interviewing.io is worth it with three interviews coming up, because the feedback is what you'll learn the most from.

turns.user: quick one, does a lender look at 2 years or 3 years of income if im self employed? i do freelance design, last year i made about 52k after expenses
turns.assistant:
Most UK and US lenders ask for two years of self-employed income, sometimes three, and they want evidence of it. That usually means tax returns or accounts for each year, plus a tax year overview or a similar statement from your accountant. Some lenders will consider one year if you've been self-employed for a shorter time and your income is strong and in the same field, but that's less common.

They'll typically average your income over the years they ask for, or use the lower of the two. So your figure of 52k is only part of the picture until you know the other year.

turns.user: what if my 2nd year was lower, like 41k. do they average it
turns.assistant:
That's the common outcome. Many lenders average the two years, which would give you about 46.5k, and some use the lower year, which would be 41k. If your income is falling year on year, a lender may look at the most recent year or use the lower number, so it's better to know which method your lender uses before you apply.

It's also worth checking whether your expenses are on your tax returns, because a lender will usually base the figure on the profit after allowable costs, not on the gross income.

turns.user: Background: I'm a single parent, take home is about 3,100 a month, daycare is 1,100 of that, and I keep ending up with nothing left by the 20th. I've heard of the 50/30/20 rule but I don't get why it's 50/30/20 and not something else. Why does it work for people?
turns.assistant:
The 50/30/20 split is a rule of thumb, not a law. The idea is to cap your three biggest categories so no one area can quietly take over your budget:

- 50% for needs, like housing, food, transport, childcare and minimum debt payments.
- 30% for wants, like eating out, subscriptions and entertainment.
- 20% for savings and extra debt payments.

It works for many people because it's simple enough to remember, and it builds saving in as a fixed step rather than leftover money. The percentages are arbitrary, but the structure forces a decision about each bucket. It doesn't work well if your needs are already very high, which can happen with childcare or high rent, because then the 50% cap is impossible to hit.

turns.user: ok so for me the needs part is already more than 50% if i count daycare. so what does the rule actually say i should do, just give up on it?
turns.assistant:
Don't give up on the structure, just change the numbers. Your needs are around 1,100 for daycare plus housing and bills, which is likely above half of your 3,100. The rule is a starting point, not a target you have to hit.

A practical version for your situation would be to let needs take what they need, then shrink the wants bucket to something small, like 10%, and put whatever is left toward savings or a buffer. Often the first fix is to look at what's in needs, like phone plans, insurance or a subscription you don't use, because small cuts there can free up real money. Then set a fixed date to move money into savings before the 20th, so it doesn't depend on what's left.

turns.user: Background: we're a 3 person team building a small invoicing tool. Right now we have customers, invoices and line items. Now we need multiple currencies, and a customer can have several billing addresses. Should currency live on the invoice or on each line item, and should addresses be their own table or just columns on customers?
turns.assistant:
Put currency on the invoice, not on each line item. An invoice is billed in one currency, so storing it per line would invite mismatches. Each line item should just store its amount in that invoice's currency.

For addresses, make a separate table with a customer_id foreign key. A customer can have several addresses, and a separate table handles that cleanly, while columns on customers would force you to fix a fixed number of slots or use messy JSON. Add a flag like is_default or a type field if you need to distinguish billing from shipping.

turns.user: ok thats what i was leaning toward. one thing: if an invoice is issued to one of the addresses, should i copy the address onto the invoice or just store a foreign key
turns.assistant:
Copy it. Store the address fields directly on the invoice as a snapshot, and you can still keep an optional reference to the original address record for convenience.

The reason is that addresses change. If a customer moves and you only store a foreign key, every old invoice would show the new address, which is wrong for legal and tax records. A snapshot means each invoice keeps the address that was actually used when it was issued. Most invoicing systems handle it this way for that reason.
